tool_args.old_string: At the per-relation level, computing EDCR for each of the 76 relation types with $\geq$5 evaluation samples reveals a more nuanced picture. Per-relation EDCR correlates strongly with per-relation Rel-F1 ($\rho = -0.793$, $p < 0.001$), confirming its utility as a difficulty indicator for individual relation types. However, per-relation EDCR is statistically independent of Evi-F1 ($\rho = -0.064$, $p = 0.58$), and Evi-F1 itself shows no association with Rel-F1 ($\rho = -0.013$, $p = 0.91$). These two null correlations establish that evidence quality and extraction ability are fully decoupled across relation types: knowing how well a model extracts a given relation tells us nothing about its evidence quality for that relation. EDCR captures this misalignment precisely because it measures the \emph{ratio} of the two capabilities rather than either in isolation. Extreme cases illustrate the diagnostic power: \texttt{date\_of\_birth} has EDCR $= 0.118$ (highly faithful, with extraction and evidence tightly coupled), while \texttt{head\_of\_government} reaches $0.956$ (highly decoupled, where the model generates accurate evidence for a relation it rarely extracts correctly). Method-level EDCR thus serves as a horizontal comparison tool across optimization paradigms, while per-relation EDCR enables vertical diagnosis of which specific relation types suffer from extraction-evidence misalignment.

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

This work formalizes evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction as a structured generation task for LLMs and provides the first systematic analysis across 85+ experimental configurations spanning four model scales, two model families, two datasets, and three post-training optimization paradigms.
Our experiments reveal three core findings.
First, RL optimization pressure and evidence-extraction decoupling severity are strongly correlated: GRPO causes catastrophic decoupling, DPO exhibits gradual degradation, and RSFT preserves stable joint performance, a relationship the EDCR diagnostic captures at method-level $\rho = -0.965$.
Second, the cost of joint evidence production follows a non-monotonic, scale-dependent pattern: 1.7B models gain +8pp Ign-F1 from evidence, 4B models pay a $-$7.5pp penalty, and 8B models approach zero cost.
Third, RSFT with NLI-based Contrastive Evidence Discrimination (CED) scoring is the only effective optimization route, yielding +4.92pp Ign-F1 over SFT at 4B scale (four-seed mean).
Our 1.7B RSFT model (50.50 Ign-F1) matches 8B SFT performance (50.51), enabling evidence-grounded extraction at a fraction of the computational cost.

Several directions remain open.
Test set evaluation on DocRED via CodaLab submission is pending and will determine whether development-set findings generalize.
The evidence grounding framework extends naturally to other information extraction tasks such as event extraction and slot filling, where output verifiability is equally critical.
Finally, iterative RSFT through multi-round self-taught reasoning may further reduce the evidence tax, particularly at the 4B scale where the penalty is most severe.

tool_args.old_string:
\section{Limitations}

All main experiments report results on the DocRED development set. Our CodaLab test set submission is pending. While dev-set tuning may overestimate absolute performance, the relative comparisons across methods (the decoupling spectrum pattern and evidence tax analysis) remain valid, as all systems are evaluated under identical conditions.

Exact-match F1, our primary metric, penalizes valid but surface-form-different entity mentions, as noted by \citet{wan2024genres}. This affects all methods equally and preserves relative comparisons, but absolute Ign-F1 numbers likely underestimate the true capability of LLM-based relation extraction.

Our per-relation EDCR analysis relies on automatic metrics. Method-level EDCR correlates strongly with Rel-F1 ($\rho{=}{-}0.965$), but a human annotation study would further validate the diagnostic value of per-relation EDCR scores.

We evaluate one algorithm per RL family: GRPO for online RL and DPO for offline preference optimization. Other algorithms (PPO, KTO) may yield different results. However, the core insight of the decoupling spectrum, that stronger gradient-based optimization pressure leads to more severe evidence decoupling, likely generalizes across algorithms within each family.

Our RSFT ablation uses four random seeds for CED scoring and two seeds for flat-NLI, which limits the statistical power of the scoring function comparison. The observed 0.02pp Rel-F1 difference between CED and flat-NLI is descriptive rather than statistically conclusive. Future work should expand seed coverage to enable formal significance testing.

CED scoring depends on an external NLI model (\texttt{cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base}) to evaluate evidence faithfulness. This introduces a pipeline dependency: CED quality is bounded by the NLI model's ability to assess entailment for relation-verbalized hypotheses, a domain that may differ from the NLI model's training distribution. Changes in the underlying NLI model could affect RSFT data selection and downstream performance.

Our experiments cover scales up to 8B parameters. The non-monotonic evidence tax pattern (positive at 1.7B, negative at 4B, near-zero at 8B) may not extrapolate to larger models (13B, 70B), where increased capacity could further reduce or eliminate the evidence generation cost. Validating the scaling trend beyond 8B remains an open question.

tool_args.old_string: We formalize evidence-grounded document-level relation extraction as a structured generation task for LLMs and conduct a systematic comparison of three post-training paradigms across 85+ configurations. Our findings reveal that RL optimization pressure correlates with evidence-extraction decoupling severity (GRPO catastrophic, DPO gradual, RSFT none; EDCR $\rho = -0.965$), and that the cost of joint evidence production follows a non-monotonic pattern across scales (+8pp at 1.7B, $-$7.5pp at 4B, near zero at 8B). RSFT with CED scoring is the only effective route, yielding +4.92pp Ign-F1 at 4B (four-seed mean), while our 1.7B RSFT model (50.50 Ign-F1) matches 8B SFT (50.51) at a fraction of the cost. The framework extends naturally to other extraction tasks where output verifiability is critical; iterative RSFT may further reduce the evidence tax at scales where it is most severe.

tool_args.old_string:
\section{Limitations}

All main experiments report results on the DocRED development set; CodaLab test set submission is pending. While dev-set tuning may overestimate absolute performance, relative comparisons across methods remain valid under identical conditions. Exact-match F1 penalizes valid but surface-form-different entity mentions~\citep{wan2024genres}, affecting all methods equally but likely underestimating absolute LLM-based extraction capability.

Our per-relation EDCR analysis relies on automatic metrics. Method-level EDCR correlates strongly with Rel-F1 ($\rho{=}{-}0.965$), but human annotation would further validate per-relation diagnostic value. The RSFT ablation uses four seeds for CED and two for flat-NLI, limiting statistical power for the 0.02pp scoring function difference.

We evaluate one algorithm per RL family (GRPO for online, DPO for offline). Other algorithms (PPO, KTO) may yield different results, though the core decoupling spectrum insight likely generalizes within each family. CED scoring depends on an external NLI model (\texttt{cross-encoder/nli-deberta-v3-base}), introducing a pipeline dependency bounded by the NLI model's entailment assessment quality on relation-verbalized hypotheses.

Our experiments cover scales up to 8B parameters. The non-monotonic evidence tax pattern may not extrapolate to larger models (13B, 70B), where increased capacity could further reduce the evidence generation cost.
